name: ความผิดปกติของวาล์ว Tricuspid
preview_text: ลิ้นหัวใจรั่วแบบเดียวกันนี้อาจมีสาเหตุมาจากความเย็นลึกในแกนกลางของร่างกาย การขาดสารอาหารเรื้อรัง หรือมีเสมหะเหนียวเกาะแน่นหน้าอก และแต่ละลิ้นก็ต้องการอาการที่แตกต่างกันโดยสิ้นเชิง
synonyms: ["Malfunction Of The Tricuspid Valve", "Tricuspid Valve Abnormality", "Tricuspid Valve Disease"]
conventional_description: The tricuspid valve sits between the right atrium and right ventricle, ensuring blood flows forward without backflow. When it malfunctions, it may leak (regurgitation) or narrow (stenosis). Common symptoms include fatigue, swelling in the legs or abdomen, a fluttering sensation in the neck, and shortness of breath with activity. Diagnosis is usually made with an echocardiogram, and the condition often accompanies right-sided heart failure or pulmonary hypertension.
conventional_treatments: Mild cases may simply be monitored. Medications like diuretics are used to reduce fluid buildup, while drugs that manage heart failure or pulmonary hypertension may also be prescribed. Severe tricuspid regurgitation or stenosis may eventually require surgical valve repair or replacement. Lifestyle adjustments, such as limiting salt intake and monitoring weight, are also standard.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, the Heart governs Blood and vessels, and it houses the Shen (spirit). A healthy tricuspid valve depends on strong Heart Qi to pump blood smoothly and on the body's ability to manage fluids without letting them pool. When the valve falters, it's rarely just a local mechanical problem - it's a sign that deeper systems are out of balance.
The Kidneys play a surprisingly central role. Kidney Yang is the body's foundational warmth, like a pilot light that drives all fluid metabolism. When this fire dims, water accumulates - often swelling the ankles and legs - and the Heart loses the warmth it needs to pump effectively. This pattern, called Disharmony between Heart and Kidneys from Kidney Yang Deficiency, is one of the most common TCM pictures behind tricuspid valve disorders, especially when cold limbs and a deep, weak pulse accompany the swelling.
But not everyone with a faulty valve feels cold and waterlogged. Some people are simply depleted: their Qi and Blood are insufficient, so the heart muscle lacks the nourishment to contract with force. They experience profound fatigue, a pale face, and palpitations that worsen after even mild exertion.
In other cases, long-standing strain causes Blood to move sluggishly through the chest, creating fixed, stabbing pain and a dusky hue to the lips and nails - a pattern of Heart Blood Stagnation.
Still others develop a sticky Phlegm obstruction in the chest, often from a weak Spleen that cannot transform fluids, leading to a heavy, suffocating sensation and a greasy tongue coat.
Because these patterns often overlap - for example, chronic Yang Deficiency can lead to secondary Blood Stagnation - TCM doesn't treat the valve in isolation. Instead, it identifies which imbalance is primary and works to restore the body's overall equilibrium, helping the heart function as well as it can within its structural limits.
classical_quote: 「心水者，其身重而少气，不得卧，烦而躁，其人阴肿。」
classical_translation: "When the Heart is affected by water qi, the body feels heavy, there is shortness of breath, an inability to lie flat, restlessness, and genital swelling. This describes right-sided heart failure with fluid overload, a classic picture of tricuspid valve dysfunction."
classical_source:
Synopsis of Prescriptions of the Golden Chamber (Jin Gui Yao Lue)  ,  Chapter 14: Pulse, Symptom Complex and Treatment of Water Qi Disease 									·

tcm_diagnosis:
A practitioner first looks for signs of cold and fluid buildup. When the legs swell, the body feels heavy, and the hands and feet are chilly even in warm weather, that points toward Disharmony between Heart and Kidneys from Kidney Yang Deficiency. The tongue is pale and puffy, often with a thin white coat, and the pulse feels deep and weak - clues that the warming fire of the Kidneys can no longer support the Heart’s pumping action.
If the main complaint is utter exhaustion with a washed‑out complexion and a fluttering heartbeat that worsens after even mild activity, Qi and Blood Deficiency is the likely picture. The tongue is pale and thin, the pulse is fine and forceless. This pattern develops gradually as the heart muscle itself becomes undernourished, leaving the whole body starved of vitality.
When chest discomfort turns into a fixed, stabbing pain, and the lips or nail beds take on a dusky hue, Heart Blood Stagnation is at play. The tongue appears dark purple with possible stasis spots, and the pulse feels choppy or wiry. Long‑standing valve strain creates this sluggish, sticky blood flow that further hinders the heart’s ability to move blood smoothly through the chambers.
A heavy, suffocating sensation in the chest - as if a weight is pressing down - combined with a thick, greasy tongue coating and a slippery pulse suggests Phlegm in the Chest. This pattern can accompany a cough with sticky phlegm and a foggy head. Here, turbid fluids congeal in the upper body, physically clogging the area around the heart and worsening the valve’s mechanical difficulty.

patterns.pattern_name: Disharmony between Heart and Kidneys caused by Kidney Yang Deficiency
patterns.symptoms: ["Aching, cold low back and knees", "Feeling of heat or agitation in the chest while the lower body feels cold", "Palpitations with a sense of fright or restlessness", "Swelling of the lower limbs and feet", "Fatigue, poor memory, and frequent clear urination"]
patterns.worse_with: Cold, raw foods and iced drinks, Overexertion and physical exhaustion, Cold, damp weather, Emotional stress and worry
patterns.better_with: Warmth applied to the lower back, Resting with legs slightly elevated, Warm, cooked meals, Moxibustion on the lower abdomen
patterns.why_this_happens: Kidney Yang is the body's foundational warmth, like a pilot light that keeps everything moving. When it weakens, it can no longer warm and propel fluids, so water accumulates - often pooling in the lower body as edema. The Heart depends on this warmth to pump effectively, and without it the tricuspid valve may struggle to close tightly, allowing blood to back up. The result is a contradictory picture: a cold, heavy lower body below, while the Heart flutters with restlessness and heat above.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, and teeth-marked with a moist white coat; the tip may be slightly redder. Pulse: deep, slow, and weak, especially at the Chi (proximal) position; the left Chi feels notably feeble.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney Yang is like a pilot light - it needs gentle, consistent warmth to stay lit. Cold foods, damp environments, and exhaustion all douse that fire, causing water to accumulate and the Heart to lose its support. Applying external warmth, eating cooked foods, and resting conserve the dwindling Yang and allow the body to slowly rekindle its foundational heat. As Kidney Yang recovers, it can once again warm the Heart, move fluids, and ease the valve's burden.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Favor warming, cooked foods like soups, stews, and congees with a pinch of ginger or cinnamon. Keep the lower back and feet warm - a hot water bottle or warm socks can make a real difference. Gentle movement like walking or tai chi helps Yang flow, but stop before exhaustion. Avoid cold, raw foods and iced drinks, which snuff out the Kidney fire further.

patterns.symptoms: ["Persistent fatigue and weakness", "Pale or sallow complexion, pale lips", "Heart palpitations, worse with exertion", "Dizziness or lightheadedness", "Poor appetite", "Spontaneous sweating"]
patterns.worse_with: Overexertion and physical exhaustion, Skipping meals or poor diet, Emotional stress and worry, Excessive sweating
patterns.better_with: Adequate rest and sleep, Warm, nourishing foods, Gentle movement like walking, Stress reduction
patterns.why_this_happens: In TCM, the Heart governs Blood and vessels. When Qi and Blood are deficient, the Heart lacks the nourishment and driving force to pump blood efficiently. This weakness can manifest as tricuspid valve dysfunction, causing palpitations, fatigue, and breathlessness because the heart struggles to maintain proper circulation.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Pale body, may be thin or have teeth marks on the edges, thin white coating. Pulse: Fine (thin) and weak, may feel empty.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Qi and Blood are the body's fundamental resources. Rest and nourishing foods allow the Spleen to produce more Qi and Blood, while overwork and stress consume them. Gentle movement stimulates circulation without draining reserves, whereas excessive exertion depletes Qi further. By conserving and replenishing, the Heart regains strength, reducing palpitations and fatigue.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked, nourishing foods like bone broths, congee with red dates and goji berries, and lightly cooked leafy greens. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that weaken the Spleen. Gentle exercise like walking or tai chi builds Qi without depleting it. Prioritize rest and sleep to allow the body to repair.

patterns.worse_with: Cold weather or drafts, Anger, frustration, or emotional stress, Fatty, greasy, or cold foods, Sedentary lifestyle
patterns.better_with: Warmth on the chest, Gentle movement like walking, Warm, cooked meals, Rest during acute pain
patterns.why_this_happens: When the tricuspid valve is damaged, the Heart's pumping grows weaker, and Blood begins to move sluggishly through the chest. Over time this stagnation creates fixed, stabbing pain and a purplish tint in the lips and nails. The stagnant Blood further impedes the valve's ability to open and close smoothly, worsening the cycle of chest oppression and breathlessness.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: dark purple body with stasis spots, distended sublingual veins, thin white coat. Pulse: choppy (涩 Sè) or knotted (结 Jié), reflecting Blood struggling to flow smoothly.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold causes Blood vessels to constrict and stagnate further, while warmth relaxes them and encourages flow. Emotional stress knots the Liver Qi, which in turn worsens Blood stasis in the chest. Gentle movement keeps Blood moving without taxing the Heart, and rest during acute pain conserves Qi so the Heart can pump more effectively.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the chest warm and avoid cold, raw foods that can congeal Blood. Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi encourages circulation without straining the Heart. Include warming, Blood-moving foods such as hawthorn, turmeric, garlic, and a little ginger tea. Manage emotional stress with deep breathing or quiet rest, as frustration and anger tend to worsen stasis.

patterns.symptoms: ["Heavy, stuffy sensation in the chest", "Coughing with abundant white, sticky phlegm", "Thick white greasy tongue coating", "Nausea or sensation of phlegm stuck in the throat", "Feeling of heaviness in the body and foggy head"]
patterns.worse_with: Damp, humid weather, Heavy, greasy, or dairy-rich meals, Sedentary lifestyle, Cold, raw foods and iced drinks
patterns.better_with: Warm, cooked meals, Gentle movement like walking, Dry, well-ventilated environment, Ginger or warm tea
patterns.why_this_happens:
When the Spleen is weak and cannot transform fluids properly, dampness accumulates and congeals into phlegm. This turbid phlegm drifts upward and settles in the chest, physically obstructing the free movement of Heart and Lung Qi.
For someone with a tricuspid valve disorder, this sticky obstruction adds a suffocating layer of resistance. The chest feels heavy and oppressed, breathing becomes labored, and the valve struggles to pump smoothly against the thickened, stagnant environment.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Pale, swollen body with teeth marks; thick white greasy coating that looks oily. Pulse: Slippery (Hua), like beads rolling under the fingers, and often slightly wiry (Xian).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Phlegm is essentially congealed dampness. Damp environments and greasy, cold foods directly feed that dampness, making the phlegm thicker and the chest heavier. Movement and warmth, on the other hand, stir Qi and activate the Spleen’s ability to transform fluids, which thins and disperses the phlegm. By keeping the body warm, dry, and gently active, you starve the phlegm of its source and help the chest breathe freely again.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid dairy, greasy foods, cold drinks, and raw vegetables, which all generate dampness and phlegm. Eat warm, cooked meals like congee with a little ginger. Gentle daily movement-like walking or tai chi-helps Qi circulate and disperse phlegm. Keep your living space dry and well-ventilated.

faqs.question: Can TCM fix a damaged tricuspid valve?
faqs.answer: TCM cannot reverse structural damage like a torn leaflet or severe calcification. However, it can significantly improve the heart's functional capacity, reduce symptoms like swelling and breathlessness, and slow the progression of the underlying imbalance. Many patients find they feel stronger and more comfortable even if the valve itself remains abnormal on echo.

faqs.question: Will I need to stop my heart medications if I start TCM?
faqs.answer: No. Never stop prescribed heart medications, especially diuretics or blood thinners, without consulting your cardiologist. TCM is used alongside conventional treatment to support your overall health. As your condition improves, your doctor may eventually adjust dosages, but this must be done under medical supervision. Always bring a complete medication list to your TCM practitioner.

faqs.question: How does acupuncture help with a valve problem?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture doesn't directly touch the valve, but it can calm the nervous system, improve circulation, and help the body shift out of the patterns that strain the heart. Points on the back, chest, and legs are selected to strengthen Heart and Kidney energy, move stagnant blood, or drain excess fluid. Many patients report feeling a deep sense of relaxation and warmth during treatment, and over time they notice less swelling and better stamina.

faqs.question: Are there any herbs I should avoid if I have tricuspid valve disease?
faqs.answer: Herbs are prescribed according to your specific pattern, so self-prescribing is risky. Some blood-moving herbs, such as Dan Shen or Hong Hua, could interact with anticoagulants. Strong stimulants like Ma Huang (ephedra) are generally avoided in heart conditions. Always work with a qualified TCM practitioner who knows your full health picture.

faqs.question: Will TCM help if I've already had valve surgery?
faqs.answer: Yes. After surgery, TCM can support recovery by building Qi and Blood, reducing post-operative fatigue, and preventing fluid re-accumulation. It's particularly helpful for addressing the constitutional weaknesses that contributed to the valve problem in the first place, which surgery alone does not correct.

faqs.question: Is TCM safe if I'm also on warfarin or other blood thinners?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture is generally safe, though your practitioner will avoid deep needling in areas prone to bruising. Many herbs that move blood or invigorate circulation may interact with warfarin, so your TCM practitioner will carefully select formulas that are compatible. Close communication between your cardiologist and TCM provider is essential.

research.title: A multicenter, randomized, double-blind, parallel-group, placebo-controlled study of the effects of qiliqiangxin capsules in patients with chronic heart failure
research.description: This large RCT enrolled 512 patients with chronic heart failure and showed that adding Qiliqiangxin capsule to standard therapy significantly reduced NT-proBNP levels, improved left ventricular ejection fraction, and enhanced quality of life compared to placebo. Many participants had functional tricuspid regurgitation, suggesting the formula's warming and diuretic effects may benefit right-sided heart dysfunction.
research.periodical: Li X, Zhang J, Huang J, et al. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2013;62(12):1065-1072.

research.title: Chinese herbal medicine for chronic heart failure: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
research.description: This meta-analysis pooled data from over 50 RCTs and found that Chinese herbal formulas, particularly those based on Zhen Wu Tang and Sheng Mai San, improved clinical symptoms, exercise tolerance, and cardiac function in heart failure patients. Although not specific to tricuspid valve disease, the results support the TCM approach of warming Yang and draining water for right-sided heart failure presentations.
research.periodical: Wang Y, et al. Front Pharmacol. 2018;9:810.
